render.title: How the ADP/ATP translocase swaps matrix ATP for cytosolic ADP
render.body:
ATP is made inside the mitochondrial matrix, but it is needed throughout the rest of the cell. The adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT, also called the ADP/ATP carrier or SLC25A4) is the protein that handles this exchange. It sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and carries out a strict one-for-one swap: one ATP out of the matrix, one ADP in from the intermembrane space (and therefore from the cytoplasm).

The exchange is electrogenic, meaning it moves a net charge across the membrane. ATP has four negative charges (ATP4-) and ADP has three negative charges (ADP3-). Each cycle exports one extra negative charge from the matrix, so the exchange is driven by the electrical component of the proton-motive force — the inside of the inner membrane is negatively charged relative to the intermembrane space, and moving ATP4- outward is thermodynamically favourable.

Mechanistically, ANT alternates between two conformations. In the "c-state" (cytoplasmic-open) the binding site faces the intermembrane space and picks up ADP3-. The protein then switches to the "m-state" (matrix-open), where the binding site faces the matrix. It releases ADP into the matrix, binds the freshly synthesised ATP4-, and flips back to the c-state to deliver ATP to the intermembrane space, from which it diffuses through the porous outer membrane into the cytoplasm.

This coupling is essential: the cell cannot benefit from mitochondrial ATP synthesis without ANT. Inhibitors such as atractyloside and bongkrekic acid block ANT by locking it in one of its two conformations, which halts the supply of cytosolic ATP and can be lethal. Because each swap costs the cell one unit of membrane potential, ANT accounts for a significant fraction of the total energetic cost of running oxidative phosphorylation.
render.summary: ANT (SLC25A4) in the inner mitochondrial membrane exchanges one ATP4- out of the matrix for one ADP3- from the cytoplasm. The exchange is electrogenic and driven by the membrane potential. The transporter alternates between two open conformations, and its inhibition blocks ATP supply to the rest of the cell.
